title: TA9-19662
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX (the claimant), is a citizen of the People's Republic of China (China). He claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsections 97(1)(a) and (b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant alleges his work in the XXXXXXXXXX left him suffering with chronic XXX XXXX pain. He attended a number of doctors with no relief. A friend, Mr. XXX at work, introduced him to the practice of Falun Gong in XXXX 2008. He found it relieved his discomfort and he began attending a Falun Gong group practice session on a weekly basis. The Public Security Bureau (PSB) arrested his friend and a number of other members of his practice group on XXXX, 2008 and it was suggested the claimant go into hiding for his own safety. The PSB attended the claimant's home on XXXX, 2008 in search of him and subsequently returned a number of times. He felt he could not remain in hiding safely and sought the assistance of a smuggler to leave the country. The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXXXX, 2009 and made a claim for refugee protection on October 02, 2009.
For the reasons that follow, I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant's testimony and the supporting documentation filed2 establish the claimant's identity as a national of China. Credibility

The determinative issue in this claim is the credibility of the claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF)3 narrative and oral testimony, concerning the claimant's identity as a genuine Falun Gong practitioner, and his pursuit by agents of the PSB. I find that the claimant was not a credible witness in this regard and is not currently wanted for arrest by the PSB on account of Falun Gong activities in China. The reasons for this decision are noted below. The hearing

In assessing credibility, the panel was mindful of the claimant's age, education, and background in China. He alleges that he has 9 years of formal education. The panel is cognizant of the many difficulties faced by a claimant in establishing a claim, including cultural factors, the milieu of the hearing room, and the stress inherent in responding to oral questions through an interpreter. The panel has taken these considerations into account in arriving at negative credibility findings. Personal Information Form omissions Can he get his Resident Identity Card?

The panel asked the claimant about the location of his Resident Identity Card (RIC). He stated that the smuggler who assisted him in leaving China took the RIC when the claimant and he left China. The smuggler was to send it to his mother, when payment for the smugglers help was received. The claimant indicated the smuggler had been paid but had not returned the card. The claimant was asked when was the last time he attempted to contact the smuggler and obtain his RIC. He replied that it was in XXXXXX 2009. The panel noted the claimant had completed his PIF October 30, 2009, but in question # 22 of the PIF, where it asks "What other identity documents do you have or could you obtain?", he did not indicate his Resident Identity Card was in China. The panel asked the claimant to comment. He replied that at that time he was not sure he could get the card back. The panel notes that the claimant swore at the opening of his hearing that his PIF was "complete, true and accurate". The panel does not find his explanation acceptable. The claimant testified that he attempted to secure the card in XXXXXX 2009, indicating there was still an expectation at the time his PIF was completed; the RIC would be sent by the smuggler. It is unreasonable to believe, if this were true, the claimant would have known his RIC was not available in October. The panel draws a negative inference to the claimant's credibility through his testimony in this situation. Where was he hiding?

The panel inquired as to the address of the friend's home where the claimant went to hide after the arrest of Mr. XXX, from his Falun Gong practice group. The claimant quickly provided the address in full, indicating he had spent one and one half months there. The panel asked why, in question 11 of his PIF4 and question 25 of his Record of Examination Form,5 did the claimant not provide the address in full as requested. The claimant stated that he had asked the interpreter and he said "that was all that was required". The panel reviewed the requirements of both forms in the "Address" portion. The panel reminded the claimant he had made extensive amendments to his PIF narrative on May 31, 2010, just prior to his hearing. The claimant was asked how he became aware the amendments to his PIF narrative were needed. He replied that he had reviewed the form with his counsel and it was suggested he make the changes. He was asked why he did not amend the address information at that time. The claimant continued to shift blame for this mistake to his "interpreter" who assisted him in filling out the form. The panel notes experienced counsel assisted the claimant and he had sworn at the opening of his hearing that his PIF was "complete, true and accurate". The panel draws an additional negative inference to the claimant's credibility through his further omission of key information from his Personal Information Form. The panel finds the claimant's omission of specific details in his PIF damaging to his ability to act as a credible witness. XXXXXXXXX Absence of Corroborating Medical Documentation

Section 106 of the IRPA and Rule 7 of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) Rules6 are clear. The claimant must provide acceptable documents establishing identity and other elements of the claim. If the claimant does not provide acceptable documents, he must explain why they were not provided, and what steps were taken to obtain them. I find, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant is in default of aspects of RPD Rule 7.

In this case, the claimant has not provided any medical documents to the Board with respect to his treatment at any medical facility or clinic in China. The claimant testified that he became interested in Falun Gong because he had a history of XXXXX problems that began in 2005 and doctors could not help him. The panel inquired as to the type of medical attention he sought for his health issues. He stated he had seen both traditional and Chinese doctors (western medicine). The panel asked the name of the medical doctor he had seen and he replied he did not know. The claimant was next asked how many times he had visited this doctor. He responded he had been to the hospital where he saw a different doctor each time on at least 10 - 20 occasions. The panel asked where the medical notes from the doctors' visits were. The claimant responded that he did not know. He further noted he had asked his mother to send them, but she could not find them. The panel asked the claimant how many times the traditional Chinese medicine doctor treated him. He stated it was 5 or 6 times. He was asked if he had notes from the traditional doctor's treatment and he replied "no". He was subsequently asked if he had receipts for his care with this doctor. He again replied "no". The panel inquired if he had made any effort to contact this doctor for a note about his XXXX condition. He responded that he did not have a note from the doctor. The claimant was asked why he had no information pertaining to his care. He stated he did not know he needed it. The panel finds the claimant's efforts to supply documentation to support an important aspect of what altered his outlook on life causing him to become "a new man" unacceptable and further damaging to his credibility. The Falun Gong practice group

The panel asked what his friend XXXXX, told the claimant about the Falun Gong practice group he belonged to. The claimant replied that Mr. XXX told him it was safe. The panel asked if his friend had told him anything else. The claimant stated his friend told him about the benefits of Faun Gong to his health. The panel rephrased the question because the claimant had not answered the question put to him. The claimant appeared hesitant. The panel prompted the claimant, asking how many members were in the group. He responded that there were eight. Next the panel asked where the group practiced. He stated his friend did not tell him. He was asked how often they practiced and answered once a week. Subsequently the claimant was questioned what day the group met and how long they practiced. He answered this question when guided. The panel asked the claimant to explain why he had not told the panel this when asked initially. He replied "I did not know you wanted to know about the group, I did not understand". The panel finds this explanation unacceptable. The hearing process was explained to the claimant shortly before this portion of testimony and he confirmed his understanding. He was told "If a question is unclear, say so and it will be rephrased. If you do not know the answer to a question, say so". The panel finds the claimant's inability to offer an answer to a basic question, which was rephrased, with out excessive guidance, detracts from his credibility. Safety precautions

The claimant was asked to provide a detailed list of all the safety precautions that his Falun Gong practice group took to avoid detection by the authorities. He stated they, used a remote location that had a front and rear door. He noted that if someone enters, the group was to stop practicing and pretend they were talking. The claimant indicated that was all. The panel prompted the claimant by asking who called and notified the group. He replied the lookouts. He was next asked if there was an escape plan for the group. He responded in the affirmative. He was subsequently asked if the group met at night. He indicated that was correct and again had to be guided by the panel to explain why this would be a safety precaution. The panel asked if the practice group had more than one location for meeting, curtains on the windows and did they have a plan to hide books if a raid by the PSB occurred. The claimant indicated his group did all of these actions to avoid detection. The panel inquired if his group was noisy during its practice. He stated they were not, but he had to be guided to explain why the group was quiet to avoid detection. The panel asked the claimant to explain why he had not mentioned the additional items in his description of the safety precautions. He responded by saying he did not know that the panel wanted all those things. The panel finds it unreasonable that the claimant having alleged that he attended the practice group once a week for approximately twelve months and took an active role, participating as a "lookout" would not be able to indicate the majority of the basic safety precautions utilized to avoid detection of his Falun Gong practice group. Working as a lookout

The claimant was asked to describe all of the activities he performed on a day he acted as a lookout for his practice group. The claimant seemed very hesitant and stated he was told by the leader to go to the back of the house and hide in a small house (shed) in an orchard. He indicated he was to call the leader if he noticed anything. The panel asked if there was anything further in procedure that he performed on that day. He replied there was not. The panel inquired if he arrived early to prepare for the task. The claimant answered that all the members arrived early. The panel rephrased the question and the claimant seemed unaware that arriving early to ensure the safety of his group was needed. He was next asked if he would check to see if the cellular phone used to call in an emergency was working and would he speak to the leader and ask if there were any special instructions. The claimant replied that the only instruction given was if he saw someone entering then he was to call. He was assisted by the panel and still did not appear to have a full understanding of the role of acting as a lookout for his Falun Gong practice group. The panel draws a further negative inference to the claimant's credibility in respect of his testimony about his actions as a lookout.

In assessing the negative inferences and credibility concerns with the claimant's oral testimony in the areas of his Falun Gong association in China, the panel finds on a balance of probabilities that he was not a member of a Falun Gong practice group in China. If the claimant was not a member of a Falun Gong practice group in China, there is no reason the PSB would be pursuing him for association with that group. The claimant may have learned the exercises associated with the practice of Falun Gong. These exercises in and of themselves are not illegal and their performance is simply analogous to the practice of Qigong, an ancient Chinese form of training for mental and physical health and does not define that individual as a genuine Falun Gong practitioner. This failure to provide trustworthy testimony is further damaging to the claimant's ability to act as a credible witness. Falun Gong Knowledge

The claimant's counsel objected on the record to the use of the text associated with the practice of Falun Gong, "Zhuan Falun"7 and written by its founder Master Li, as reference material for questioning during the hearing. The claimant indicated in his PIF narrative that he had read and studied the text and confirmed this in testimony during the hearing. The panel notes that information sworn to, as well as, testimony provided by the claimant at the hearing, is available for investigation and questioning during the course of the hearing.

The panel confirmed the claimant alleged he had been practicing Falun Gong for two years and he was reading the key text of Falun Gong, Zhuan Falun8, for the third time. The claimant was asked a series of questions to assist in the consideration of his identification as a genuine Falun Gong practitioner. He was asked the significance of the date May 13 to Falun Gong practitioners. He answered that this was the birthday of Master Li, the founder of Falun Gong. The panel inquired if there was anything else associated with this date. The claimant did not know and the panel identified it was the birth date of the founder of Buddhism. The claimant identified that Master Li lives in the United States, but was not able to identify the year he left China, stating it was the same year that Falun Gong was banned in China (which the panel identified as 1999). The panel informed the claimant that 1996 was the correct answer and he replied that he thought it was 1997. These dates are important milestones for any Falun Gong practitioner and it is not unreasonable that the claimant would be familiar with them. The claimant was asked if he was familiar with the concept of the "third eye" and he indicated he had read about it. He was able to identify the fact that Master Li opened the "third eye" and that it allowed practitioners to see "things ordinary people can't see" He was asked to further explain the concept of the "third eye" and seemed perplexed. He attempted to describe the five levels of the third eye, but became confused, naming three correctly, but did not know what made these levels different. The panel sensed the claimant's difficulty and asked if he had a favourite "talk" from the text Zhuan Falun. He identified "Talk Seven". He was asked if he could explain to the panel about the contents of that talk. The claimant stated the talk discussed "killing". He was informed this was correct and asked if anything else was discussed in the "talk". The claimant answered that he did not know. The panel assisted the claimant by indicating he had mentioned a topic earlier in testimony. The claimant then identified "eating meat" as another area of "Talk Seven". The claimant was unable to identify any other aspect of "Talk Seven", an area he indicated he had an interest in and knowledge of. The panel next asked the claimant what Master Li states about individuals who just perform the exercises associated with Falun Gong. He replied "you are not taking people to a higher level". The panel replied that this was not correct and answered "if one exercises and fails to understand the philosophies of Falun Gong they are not disciples of Falun Gong at all". The claimant stated he had "heard this". The panel asked the claimant a few more questions about the concept of the "falun", which he was able to answer correctly. He was able to properly explain how the concept of healing taught by Master Li, worked with his personal health problem.

The claimant possessed some knowledge of the philosophical concepts of the Falun Gong discipline and the content of Zhuan Falun, but he often required prompting to provide responses to questions and his answers frequently indicated a lack of depth of understanding.

Master Li the founder of Falun Gong notes that without an understanding of the philosophy of Falun Gong (fundamental knowledge essential for the task of undertaking proper cultivation towards higher stages of attainment), the exercises associated with Falun Gong are solely Qi Gong exercises.9 The performance of these exercises in and of themselves is not illegal in China. Knowledge of the philosophy gained through study of the texts associated with the Falun Gong discipline is a key component of being a member of the Falun Gong discipline. In assessing the claimant's knowledge of Falun Gong principles and philosophy, the panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the claimant is not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner.

The claimant submitted a note from two associates at a Falun Gong practice group in Toronto and a series of photographs taken of the claimant allegedly practicing and participating in Falun Gong group activity. The photographs indicate only that the claimant was at these locations and participated at the time of the pictures. There are many of these celebrations and activities held each year in the Toronto area forming an important part of the Falun Gong philosophy. No evidence was provided of actual attendance and participation at the events. The notes (obtained just prior to his refugee hearing) from alleged Falun Gong practitioners are on plain paper, with no verification of identity or qualification as genuine Falun Gong practitioners. The claimant has not provided letters identifying his associates or himself, from the Falun Dafa Association of Toronto, a recognized organization which attests to identification of Falun Gong practitioners. The panel will assign this evidence the appropriate weight. Summary

It is difficult to make a judgment regarding the genuineness of a persons' philosophical practice. However, on the basis of the findings and negative inferences noted herein, the claimant has failed to act as a credible witness in his claim. In Sheikh,10 MacGuigan, J.A., writing for the court, stated, in part: "In other words a general finding of a lack of credibility on the part of the applicant may conceivably extend to all relevant information emanating from his testimony."

On a balance of probabilities, the panel has found that the claimant was not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in China or in Canada. Whatever knowledge of Falun Gong the claimant now possesses was obtained only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim.

The panel has considered all three protection grounds under section 96 and sub-section 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and, on the basis of the totality of all the evidence made available to the panel, finds that there is not a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted in China, nor that he would be subjected personally to a risk to his life, cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture. For these reasons, the claim is rejected. (signed) "R. Bebbington" R.
